entries.17:4: Hoshea tried to get help from Egypt and stopped paying tribute, so the Assyrian king found out and threw him in prison. Trusting the wrong ally and breaking his word cost him his freedom.
entries.17:5: The Assyrian king then marched through the land and surrounded Samaria, the capital, for three years. The siege was long and devastating for the people.
entries.17:6: In Hoshea's ninth year the Assyrians captured Samaria and deported the Israelites to distant lands. This was the end of the northern kingdom as a nation in its own land.
entries.17:7: The writer explains that this disaster happened because Israel sinned against the God who had rescued them from slavery in Egypt and had turned to other gods. Their downfall was not bad luck but the result of turning away from the one who saved them.
entries.17:8: They copied the customs of the nations God had driven out before them. Adopting the practices of those who rejected God led them away from him.
entries.17:9: The Israelites did wrong things in secret against the Lord and built places of worship all over the land, from small watchtowers to walled cities. Their disobedience was widespread and hidden.
entries.17:10: They set up stone and wooden pillars for worship on every high hill and under every green tree. They were imitating pagan worship everywhere they went.
entries.17:11: They burned offerings at these high places just as the nations God had removed had done, and this made the Lord angry. They were following the very patterns God had warned against.
entries.17:12: They served worthless idols even though the Lord had plainly told them not to. God had already made his will clear, so their idolatry was deliberate disobedience.
entries.17:13: God repeatedly warned Israel and Judah through his prophets, calling them to turn from their evil ways and obey his law. God was patient and gave them many chances to come back.
entries.17:14: But they refused to listen and became stubborn, just like their ancestors who did not trust the Lord. Stubbornness against God's warnings kept them from turning back.
entries.17:15: They rejected God's rules and the covenant he made with their ancestors, chasing worthless things and becoming foolish like the nations around them. Rejecting God's word made them empty and confused.
entries.17:16: They abandoned all the Lord's commands, made metal idols and an Asherah pole, worshipped the stars, and served Baal. They replaced the worship of God with every kind of false worship.
entries.17:17: They even sacrificed their own children in fire and practiced sorcery and divination, doing evil until the Lord was provoked to anger. Their sin had become deeply cruel and corrupt.
entries.17:18: So the Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them from his presence, leaving only Judah. Persistent sin finally brought the judgment God had warned about.
entries.17:19: Even Judah did not keep the Lord's commands but followed the same practices Israel had made. Judah was not innocent either, despite being spared for a time.
entries.17:20: So the Lord rejected all the people of Israel, brought trouble on them, and handed them over to their enemies until he removed them from his sight. God's patience had run out after generations of rebellion.
entries.17:21: Israel had split from the house of David and made Jeroboam king, and he led them away from the Lord's laws into great sin. The division became a spiritual disaster that shaped everything after.
entries.17:22: The Israelites kept committing the same sins Jeroboam had introduced and never turned away from them. They persisted in the pattern their leaders had set.
entries.17:23: Finally the Lord removed Israel from his presence, just as the prophets had said, and they were taken to Assyria, where they remained. The exile was the fulfillment of long-standing warnings.
entries.17:24: The Assyrian king brought people from several other nations to settle in the towns of Samaria in place of the Israelites. The land was repopulated with foreigners who did not know the Lord.
entries.17:25: At first these new settlers did not worship the Lord, so he sent lions among them and some died. God made it clear that the land belonged to him and demanded reverence.
entries.17:26: The settlers told the Assyrian king that they did not know how the god of the land was to be worshipped, and that this was why the lions were killing them. They recognized something was wrong but did not know the true God.
entries.17:27: The Assyrian king ordered that one of the exiled Israelite priests be sent back to teach the settlers how to worship the god of the land. Even a pagan ruler acknowledged that the people needed instruction.
entries.17:28: So one of the priests taken from Samaria returned and lived in Bethel, teaching the settlers how to worship the Lord. Instruction was given, but it was mixed with the old idolatry.
entries.17:29: Each group of settlers made its own gods and placed them in the high places the Samaritans had built, each nation in its own town. Instead of true worship, they added the Lord to their collection of gods.
entries.17:30: The people from Babylon made Succoth-benoth, those from Cuth made Nergal, and those from Hamath made Ashima. Each group brought its own idols with it.
entries.17:31: The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children as sacrifices to Adrammelech and Anammelech. Their worship included horrifying practices.
entries.17:32: They also worshipped the Lord and appointed priests from among themselves to offer sacrifices at the high places. Their religion was a mixture of devotion to God and to idols.
entries.17:33: They worshipped the Lord but also honored their own gods, following the customs of the nations they came from. This divided loyalty was not true worship of God at all.
entries.17:34: To this day they continue in their old ways, not truly worshipping the Lord or keeping his commands and law given to the descendants of Jacob. Their religion looked religious but was not obedience to God.
entries.17:35: The Lord had made a covenant with them and commanded them to have no other gods, not to worship or serve them or offer sacrifices to them. God's covenant was exclusive and clear.
entries.17:36: The Lord, who brought them out of Egypt with great power, is the one they must worship and sacrifice to. He alone had proven himself worthy of their devotion.
entries.17:37: They were to keep and obey forever the rules, commands, and law God had written for them, and have no other gods. God's instructions were not optional or temporary.
entries.17:38: They were to remember the covenant God made with them and have no other gods. Remembering God's covenant means refusing to give loyalty to anything else.
entries.17:39: They were to worship the Lord their God, because he is the one who would save them from all their enemies. Only God could give them real security and deliverance.
entries.17:40: But they paid no attention and continued in their old ways. The chapter ends with the sad reality that the people refused to listen to God's clear commands.
entries.17:41: These people claimed to worship God while still holding on to their idols, and that mixed loyalty got passed down through the family. It's a warning that what we tolerate in our own lives can become the pattern our children follow.
entries.18:1: This verse marks the moment Hezekiah became king of Judah, dated by the reign of Israel's king Hoshea. It reminds the reader that God's story moves through real people and real dates, not vague legend.
entries.18:2: Hezekiah was twenty-five when he took the throne and ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem; his mother's name is recorded too. The details show he was a real historical king whose life and choices are open before God.
entries.18:3: Hezekiah did what was right in God's eyes, following the example of David. It shows that a person's life can be measured by faithfulness to God rather than by success or popularity.
entries.18:4: Hezekiah removed the local shrines, smashed the sacred stones, cut down the Asherah pole, and destroyed the bronze snake Moses had made because people were burning offerings to it. Good reform means removing even old religious things that have become objects of worship instead of God.
entries.18:5: Hezekiah trusted the Lord, the God of Israel, more than any king of Judah before him. The verse shows that wholehearted trust in God is what makes a life stand out.
entries.18:6: He held firmly to the Lord, did not turn away from following him, and kept the commands God gave through Moses. Steady obedience, not just occasional good deeds, is what faithfulness looks like.
entries.18:7: The Lord was with Hezekiah, so he prospered, and he rebelled against the king of Assyria instead of serving him. When God is with someone, they can stand up to powers that once controlled them.
entries.18:8: He defeated the Philistines all the way to Gaza and its territory. This shows God giving him victory over long-standing enemies of his people.
entries.18:9: In Hezekiah's fourth year, the Assyrian king Shalmaneser attacked Samaria and besieged it. The verse sets the stage for judgment on the northern kingdom of Israel.
entries.18:10: After three years the siege ended and Samaria fell, in Hezekiah's sixth year and Hoshea's ninth. It shows that God's warnings about judgment came true exactly as stated.
entries.18:11: The Assyrian king deported the people of Israel to Assyria and settled them in Halah, Habor by the Gozan River, and the towns of the Medes. Exile was the real consequence of the nation's long rejection of God.
entries.18:12: This happened because Israel did not listen to the Lord their God but broke his covenant and disobeyed all that Moses commanded. It is a sober warning that ignoring God's voice has serious results.
entries.18:13: In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Sennacherib of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified towns of Judah. Even a faithful king could still face overwhelming military pressure.
entries.18:14: Hezekiah admitted fault and asked the Assyrian king to stop attacking, agreeing to pay whatever was demanded, which was set at three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold. It shows the heavy cost of buying off a powerful enemy.
entries.18:15: Hezekiah paid the silver from the Lord's temple and from the royal treasury. The verse shows how a national crisis drained even the resources dedicated to God.
entries.18:16: Hezekiah cut the gold off the temple doors and doorposts he had overlaid and gave it to the Assyrian king. It shows how desperate the situation had become, even to the point of stripping the temple.
entries.18:17: The Assyrian king sent three high officials with a strong army from Lachish to Jerusalem, and they stationed themselves by the upper pool on the washerman's road. The pressure on Jerusalem was now direct and public.
entries.18:18: They called for the king, and three of Hezekiah's officials—Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah—came out to meet them. The verse shows the tense negotiation between a threatened nation and its enemy.
entries.18:19: The Assyrian official told them to tell Hezekiah that the great king of Assyria asks what he is relying on. It is a taunt meant to shake the king's confidence.
entries.18:20: He says that talk of plans and military strength is empty unless there is someone real to back it up, and asks who Hezekiah is trusting. It exposes the gap between confident words and actual support.
entries.18:21: He compares Egypt to a splintered reed that pierces the hand of anyone leaning on it, saying Pharaoh is just as unreliable to those who trust him. It warns against putting hope in powerful allies who cannot deliver.
entries.18:22: He claims that if they trust the Lord, Hezekiah has offended him by removing the high places and altars and restricting worship to Jerusalem. The taunt twists the truth, since those removals were actually obedience to God.
entries.18:23: He offers a wager: if Hezekiah can supply riders, the Assyrian king will give him two thousand horses. It is mockery of Judah's lack of military strength.
entries.18:24: He asks how Judah could even repel the least of Assyria's officers when they are depending on Egypt for chariots and horsemen. The point is to make Judah feel hopelessly outmatched.
entries.18:25: He claims he has come to destroy this place with the Lord's own authority, saying the Lord told him to attack the land. It is a bold claim that mixes truth and bluff to intimidate.
entries.18:26: Hezekiah's officials asked the Assyrian to speak Aramaic so the people on the wall would not understand. They wanted to keep the frightening threats from spreading panic.
entries.18:27: The Assyrian refused, saying he was sent to speak to the men on the wall too, who would suffer hunger and thirst during a siege. He deliberately aimed his words at the ordinary people to break their morale.
entries.18:28: He then stood and shouted loudly in Hebrew so everyone could hear the words of the great king of Assyria. The intimidation was now aimed directly at the whole city.
entries.18:29: He told the people not to let Hezekiah deceive them, because Hezekiah could not save them. It is a direct attack on the people's trust in their leader.
entries.18:30: He warned them not to let Hezekiah make them trust the Lord with promises that the city would be safe. The enemy's strategy was to undermine confidence in God himself.
entries.18:31: He urged them not to listen to Hezekiah but to make peace with Assyria and come out, promising each person could eat from his own vine and fig tree and drink from his own well. It offered a tempting picture of safety in surrender.
entries.18:32: He promised to take them to a land like their own, full of grain, wine, bread, olives, and honey, so they would live and not die, and again warned them not to trust Hezekiah's claim that the Lord would save them. The offer sounded generous but meant exile from home and from God's city.
entries.18:33: He asked whether any god of the nations had ever kept its land from the Assyrian king. It is an argument from history meant to make the Lord seem no different from powerless idols.
entries.18:34: He listed the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah and asked where they were, and whether they had saved Samaria. The taunt assumed all gods were alike and equally defeated.
entries.18:35: He asked which of all these gods had saved its country from him, so why should anyone think the Lord would save Jerusalem. It is the climax of the intimidation, directly challenging God's power.
entries.18:36: The people stayed silent and gave no answer, because the king had ordered them not to respond. Silence here was disciplined obedience, not agreement with the enemy.
entries.18:37: Hezekiah's officials came to him with their clothes torn in grief and told him everything the Assyrian official had said. The verse shows the shock and sorrow the threats caused, and sets up the king's response.
entries.19:1: When the king heard the threats, he was deeply shaken and humbled himself before God, going to the temple to pray. It shows that turning to God in a crisis is the right first response.
entries.19:2: Hezekiah sent his top officials and priests, also dressed in mourning, to ask the prophet Isaiah for God's word. It means the leaders sought God's guidance together rather than relying on themselves.
entries.19:3: Hezekiah describes the situation as a time of deep distress and disgrace, like a mother too weak to give birth. It means the nation is in desperate trouble and needs God's help to survive.
entries.19:4: Hezekiah hopes God will hear the enemy's insults against the living God and act, and he asks Isaiah to pray for the remaining people. It means we can bring insults against God's name to him and ask others to pray with us.
entries.19:5: The officials simply did what the king told them and delivered his message to Isaiah. It shows the ordinary step of obeying and seeking God's word in a crisis.
entries.19:6: God's answer through Isaiah is that Hezekiah should not be afraid of the insulting words the Assyrian officials spoke. It means God hears threats against him and tells his people not to be shaken by them.
entries.19:7: God promises to stir the enemy king to hear alarming news, return home, and be killed there by the sword. It means God himself will deal with the threat and turn the enemy back.
entries.19:8: The Assyrian official returned and found his king had moved on to attack another town. It shows the enemy's plans were already shifting, just as God had said.
entries.19:9: When the Assyrian king heard that Ethiopia's king was marching against him, he sent another threatening message to Hezekiah. It means pressure came again even after a brief pause, testing the king's trust in God.
entries.19:10: The message warns Hezekiah not to let his God give him false hope that Jerusalem will be spared. It means the enemy tries to undermine trust in God's promises by suggesting they are empty.
entries.19:11: The king reminds Hezekiah of how Assyria has destroyed every land it attacked and asks why he would be any different. It means the enemy uses fear and past victories to make God's people feel hopeless.
entries.19:12: He lists nations whose gods failed to save them from his ancestors. It means he assumes Israel's God is just another powerless god like the rest.
entries.19:13: He names more defeated kings and towns, pressing the same point that no one has escaped him. It means the intimidation is repeated to wear down Hezekiah's confidence.
entries.19:14: Hezekiah took the letter, read it, then went up to the temple and spread it out before the Lord. It means he brought the threat honestly and openly to God in prayer.
entries.19:15: Hezekiah prays to the Lord, who is enthroned above the cherubim, declaring that he alone is God over all kingdoms and made heaven and earth. It means prayer begins by remembering who God truly is.
entries.19:16: He asks God to listen and see, and to take note of the insults Sennacherib has spoken against the living God. It means we can ask God to pay attention to the wrong done against his name.
entries.19:17: Hezekiah admits the Assyrian kings really have destroyed nations and their lands. It means honest prayer acknowledges the facts rather than pretending the danger isn't real.
entries.19:18: He explains those nations' gods were only wood and stone made by human hands, so they could be burned. It means the enemy's gods were never real, unlike the living God.
entries.19:19: He asks God to save them so that all the kingdoms of the earth will know that the Lord alone is God. It means the goal of rescue is that God's name be honoured before the world.
entries.19:20: Isaiah sends word that God has heard Hezekiah's prayer against Sennacherib. It means God listens when his people pray and answers through his prophet.
entries.19:21: God's word says Jerusalem, pictured as a young woman, despises and mocks the Assyrian king. It means the proud enemy who seemed so strong is actually a laughingstock before God's people.
entries.19:22: God asks whom the king has insulted and spoken proudly against, and the answer is the Holy One of Israel. It means mocking God's people is really mocking God himself.
entries.19:23: The king boasted that with his chariots he had climbed mountains and cut down Lebanon's finest cedars. It means his pride was enormous, claiming power over everything.
entries.19:24: He boasted of digging wells in foreign lands and drying up Egypt's rivers with his feet. It means he claimed total control over water and nations, an arrogant exaggeration.
entries.19:25: God says he planned all this long ago and now brought it about, using Assyria to turn strong cities into ruins. It means the enemy was only a tool in God's hands, not the real power.
entries.19:26: Their people had no strength and were crushed like grass on a roof that dries up quickly. It means the defeated nations were weak and short-lived, not because Assyria was invincible.
entries.19:27: God says he knows everything about the Assyrian king, his sitting down and rising up, his coming and going. It means no one is hidden from God, not even the mightiest ruler.
entries.19:28: Because of his rage and pride, God will put a hook in his nose and a cord in his lips and send him back the way he came. It means God will restrain and turn back the proud enemy like an animal on a leash.
entries.19:29: God gives a sign: for two years the people will eat what grows by itself, and in the third year they will plant and harvest and plant vineyards. It means God will provide for them through the recovery period.
entries.19:30: The survivors of Judah will take root again and bear fruit. It means God promises lasting restoration, not just survival.
entries.19:31: A remnant will come out of Jerusalem and Mount Zion, and the Lord of armies will accomplish this. It means God's purpose guarantees that his people will continue.
entries.19:32: God says the Assyrian king will not enter the city, shoot an arrow at it, or build siege works against it. It means the threat will not touch Jerusalem at all.
entries.19:33: He will go back the same way he came and will not enter the city, says the Lord. It means God's word is definite: the enemy's advance stops here.
entries.19:34: God will defend the city for his own honour and for the sake of his servant David. It means God's protection rests on his own name and his promises, not on the people's strength.
entries.19:35: That night the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 in the Assyrian army, and in the morning there were only dead bodies. It means God himself defeated the enemy without any battle.
entries.19:36: Sennacherib, the Assyrian king, withdrew and went back to Nineveh. It means the threat was over and the enemy retreated just as God had promised.
entries.19:37: While he was worshipping his god Nisroch, his own sons killed him with swords and fled, and another son took the throne. It means the proud king met the violent end God had foretold, in the very place of his false worship.
entries.20:1: Hezekiah was very sick and close to dying, so the prophet Isaiah told him to get his affairs in order because he would not recover. It reminds readers that death can come sooner than expected, so we should be ready.
entries.20:2: Hezekiah turned away to face the wall and prayed to the Lord. It shows that when we are in deep distress, we can turn to God honestly and privately.
entries.20:3: Hezekiah asked God to remember how faithfully and wholeheartedly he had lived, and then he cried bitterly. It shows that pouring out our grief and asking God to remember our devotion is a normal part of prayer.
entries.20:4: Before Isaiah had even left the area, God gave him a new message. It shows that God can answer prayer quickly, even before we expect it.
entries.20:5: God told Isaiah to go back and tell Hezekiah that he had heard his prayer and seen his tears, and that he would be healed and back at the temple in three days. It shows that God notices our sorrow and responds to sincere prayer.
entries.20:6: God promised Hezekiah fifteen more years of life and protection for the city from Assyria, for the sake of his own honor and his promise to David. It shows that God's help rests on his own faithfulness, not just on our worthiness.
entries.20:7: Isaiah told them to put a fig cake on Hezekiah's wound, and he recovered. It shows that God often works through simple, practical means alongside his promise of healing.
entries.20:8: Hezekiah asked Isaiah for a sign confirming that God would heal him and that he would go to the temple on the third day. It shows that asking God for reassurance is not wrong when our faith feels weak.
entries.20:9: Isaiah offered Hezekiah a choice of sign: whether the shadow would move forward ten steps or backward. It shows God graciously offering confirmation in a way suited to the person asking.
entries.20:10: Hezekiah said moving forward is easy, so let the shadow go backward ten steps instead. It shows he wanted a sign that clearly could not happen by ordinary means.
entries.20:11: Isaiah prayed, and God made the shadow go back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz. It shows that God is sovereign over nature and confirms his word with unmistakable signs.
entries.20:12: The king of Babylon sent messengers with a gift to Hezekiah after hearing he had been sick. It shows that news of God's work can reach far places, but also sets up a test of Hezekiah's wisdom.
entries.20:13: Hezekiah welcomed the messengers and proudly showed them all his wealth, weapons, and treasures, holding nothing back. It shows how easily success and flattery can lead us to boast instead of giving glory to God.
entries.20:14: Isaiah asked Hezekiah what the men had said and where they came from, and Hezekiah answered that they came from distant Babylon. It shows that God was giving Hezekiah a chance to reflect on what he had done.
entries.20:15: Isaiah asked what the visitors had seen, and Hezekiah admitted they had seen everything in his house. It shows that his pride had exposed his whole kingdom to a foreign power.
entries.20:16: Isaiah told Hezekiah to listen to what the Lord was about to say. It shows that God's word must be heard even when it is unwelcome news.
entries.20:17: God said that a time was coming when everything in Hezekiah's house and all his ancestors' treasures would be carried off to Babylon. It shows that pride and careless exposure can lead to serious loss, even generations later.
entries.20:18: God also said that some of Hezekiah's own sons would be taken away and made servants in the Babylonian king's palace. It shows that the consequences of a leader's choices can fall on their family.
entries.20:19: Hezekiah accepted God's word as good and was relieved that there would be peace and security in his own lifetime. It shows how easy it is to accept judgment when it does not personally cost us much.
entries.20:20: The rest of Hezekiah's achievements, including how he built the pool and water channel, are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings. It shows that his practical work for the city was remembered alongside his spiritual life.
entries.20:21: Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king. It shows that even a faithful king's life ends, and the story passes to the next generation.
entries.21:1: Manasseh became king of Judah at just twelve years old and ruled for fifty-five years, longer than any other king. His long reign shows that God can be patient even when a leader does terrible things.
entries.21:2: Manasseh did what God considered evil, copying the wicked practices of the nations God had driven out before Israel. A leader's choices can pull a whole people away from God.
entries.21:3: He rebuilt the idol shrines his father Hezekiah had torn down and set up altars to false gods like Baal and the stars. He undid the good his father had done and led people back into idol worship.
entries.21:4: He placed idols right inside the Lord's temple, the very place God had chosen for his own name. This shows how far he went in disrespecting God's house.
entries.21:5: He built altars to the stars in the temple courtyards, turning God's own courts into places of idol worship. He filled the space meant for worshiping God with worship of false gods.
entries.21:6: He sacrificed his own son in fire and practiced fortune-telling and consulted mediums, doing much evil that angered the Lord. This shows how deeply sin can corrupt a person's choices, even toward their own family.
entries.21:7: He set up a carved image of the goddess Asherah inside the temple where God had promised his name would remain forever. He directly challenged God's promise by putting an idol where God said he would dwell.
entries.21:8: God promised Israel would never again be forced out of their land if they carefully obeyed all his commands. God's blessing was tied to their obedience, not just his promise.
entries.21:9: The people refused to listen, and Manasseh led them into worse evil than the nations God had removed before them. A bad leader can make a whole nation worse than those who never knew God.
entries.21:10: God spoke to the people through his prophets, his chosen messengers. God does not stay silent about sin; he warns people through those he sends.
entries.21:11: God said Manasseh had done worse evil than the Amorites before him and had led Judah into idol worship. God sees and names the sin of leaders who cause others to sin.
entries.21:12: God announced he would bring such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that everyone who heard about it would be stunned. Sin brings real consequences, and God's judgment would be shocking.
entries.21:13: God would measure Jerusalem by the same standard he used on Samaria and Ahab's family, wiping it clean like a washed plate turned upside down. God judges all nations by the same standard of justice.
entries.21:14: God said he would reject the remnant of his people and hand them over to their enemies, who would plunder them. Persistent sin can lead to losing God's protection.
entries.21:15: God said this would happen because his people had done evil and angered him from the day they left Egypt until now. Long patterns of sin, not just one mistake, brought this judgment.
entries.21:16: Manasseh also killed many innocent people until Jerusalem was full of blood, on top of his other sins. A leader's evil can cause terrible harm to ordinary, innocent people.
entries.21:17: The rest of Manasseh's deeds and sins are recorded in the official history book of Judah's kings. His story was written down, showing that human records keep account of what leaders do.
entries.21:18: Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his palace, and his son Amon became king. Even a long, powerful reign ends in death, and the next generation takes over.
entries.21:19: Amon became king at twenty-two and ruled only two years in Jerusalem; his mother was Meshullemeth. His short reign stands in sharp contrast to his father's long one.
entries.21:20: Amon did evil in God's eyes, just as his father Manasseh had done. Children often follow the example of their parents, for good or for bad.
entries.21:21: He followed all his father's ways, serving and worshiping the same false gods his father had served. He chose to copy his father's idolatry rather than learn from his mistakes.
entries.21:22: He turned away from the Lord, the God of his ancestors, and did not walk in God's ways. Rejecting the God your family once knew is a serious choice.
entries.21:23: Amon's own servants plotted against him and killed him in his own house. Even a king is not safe from betrayal when his rule is built on evil.
entries.21:24: The people of the land executed everyone involved in the plot against the king and made his son Josiah king. Ordinary people stepped in to restore order and set up the next king.
entries.21:25: The rest of Amon's deeds are recorded in the official history book of Judah's kings. His actions were written down and remembered, just like his father's.
entries.21:26: Amon was buried in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah became king in his place. Despite a wicked father, Josiah would become one of Judah's best kings, showing that a person's path is not fixed by their family.
entries.22:1: Josiah became king of Judah when he was only eight years old and ruled for thirty-one years. His story shows that even a young person can be given real responsibility and used by God.
entries.22:2: Josiah did what pleased the Lord and followed the example of King David, not swerving off the right path. This encourages the reader to stay faithful and consistent in doing right, even from a young age.
entries.22:3: In the eighteenth year of his reign, Josiah sent his secretary Shaphan to the temple. This shows a king taking practical steps to care for God's house.
entries.22:4: Josiah told Shaphan to have the high priest collect the money that had been gathered from the people at the temple. It shows the king organizing the repair of God's house with the resources people had given.
entries.22:5: The money was to be handed to the supervisors so they could pay the workers repairing the temple. Good leadership means making sure resources actually reach the people doing the work.
entries.22:6: The funds went to carpenters, builders, and stonecutters, and to buy timber and stone for the repairs. This is ordinary, practical work that keeps a place of worship in good condition.
entries.22:7: The workers did not have to account for the money because they were trusted to handle it honestly. This shows the value of trusting people who have proven to be faithful.
entries.22:8: The high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple and gave it to Shaphan. It reminds the reader that God's word can be lost or neglected and then rediscovered, changing everything.
entries.22:9: Shaphan reported back to the king that the money had been paid out and the work was underway. Honest reporting keeps leaders informed and builds trust.
entries.22:10: Shaphan then told the king that Hilkiah had found a book and read it aloud to him. Reading God's word aloud to those in authority can have a powerful effect.
entries.22:11: When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes in grief. This shows that God's word should move us deeply when we realize how far we have fallen short.
entries.22:12: Josiah gave orders to the priest, his officials, and his servants to act on what had been read. A good response to God's word includes involving others and taking action.
entries.22:13: Josiah wanted the Lord's guidance for himself and the whole nation because he feared God's anger over their disobedience. It is wise to seek God's direction when we realize we have been ignoring his word.
entries.22:14: The king's men went to Huldah, a woman prophet, to ask the Lord's answer. God can speak through anyone he chooses, and it is right to seek his word humbly.
entries.22:15: Huldah told them to take the Lord's message back to the man who sent them. God's word comes with authority and is meant to be delivered faithfully.
entries.22:16: The Lord said he would bring disaster on Jerusalem and its people, just as the book warned. Ignoring God's word has real consequences, both for individuals and for a whole society.
entries.22:17: The people had abandoned the Lord and worshiped other gods, so his anger would not be turned aside. This shows that turning away from God is serious and brings judgment.
entries.22:18: The Lord had a separate message for King Josiah, who had sent them to seek him. God notices when a person sincerely seeks him, even in the middle of a nation's failure.
entries.22:19: Because Josiah humbled himself and wept over the warnings, the Lord heard him. God responds with mercy to those who take his word seriously and grieve over sin.
entries.22:20: The Lord promised Josiah would die in peace and not see the disaster coming on the city. God's mercy spared him personally, even though judgment on the nation was still certain.
entries.23:1: The king called together all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem to meet with him. It shows that big changes were about to be announced to the whole nation, not just a few people.
entries.23:2: The king went to the temple and read the lost book of God's law out loud to everyone, from important leaders to ordinary people. Everyone, no matter how small, needed to hear what God had said.
entries.23:3: The king stood and made a solemn promise to follow the Lord and obey his commands with his whole heart, and the people agreed to do the same. It was a public commitment to take God's word seriously.
entries.23:4: The king ordered the priests to remove all the objects used for worshiping false gods from the temple, and he had them burned outside the city. He was cleaning out God's house of everything that dishonored him.
entries.23:5: He removed the priests who had been appointed to burn offerings to false gods like Baal, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He stopped the practice of worshiping created things instead of the Creator.
entries.23:6: He took the Asherah idol out of the temple, burned it, crushed it to dust, and scattered the dust over graves. He was treating the idol as something worthless and unclean.
entries.23:7: He tore down the rooms in the temple where people had been used for sexual worship and where women made robes for the idol. He was removing the shameful practices that had taken over God's house.
entries.23:8: He brought the priests from the towns of Judah to Jerusalem and made the places where they had worshiped false gods unfit for use, from one end of the land to the other. He was shutting down the wrong places of worship everywhere.
entries.23:9: These priests were not allowed to serve at the Lord's altar in Jerusalem, but they were still given food to eat with the other priests. They were treated fairly even though they could not serve.
entries.23:10: He made the place called Topheth unfit for use so that no one could burn their children as offerings to the false god Molech. He was stopping a terrible practice that harmed children.
entries.23:11: He removed the horses and chariots that the kings had dedicated to the sun god and burned the chariots. He was getting rid of everything connected to sun worship.
entries.23:12: He tore down the altars that earlier kings had built on the roof and in the temple courtyards, crushed them, and threw the dust into the stream. He was undoing the wrong things previous kings had done.
entries.23:13: He made unfit the places of worship that Solomon had built for the false gods of other nations. Even a wise king's mistakes had to be corrected.
entries.23:14: He broke the stone and wooden pillars used in false worship and filled the places with human bones, which made them ceremonially unclean. He was making sure those places could never be used for worship again.
entries.23:15: He destroyed the altar and high place at Bethel that Jeroboam had built, which had led Israel into sin, burning and crushing it to dust. He was removing a long-standing source of idolatry.
entries.23:16: Josiah took bones from the nearby graves and burned them on the altar to make it unclean, just as a prophet had predicted long before. This showed that God's words spoken years earlier came true.
entries.23:17: Josiah asked whose tombstone he was seeing, and the people told him it belonged to the prophet who had predicted what he was doing. He wanted to know the story behind the grave.
entries.23:18: He ordered that the prophet's bones not be disturbed, so they stayed with the bones of another prophet from Samaria. He showed respect for the man who had spoken God's truth.
entries.23:19: Josiah also destroyed the high places in the towns of Samaria that the kings of Israel had built, doing the same as he had done at Bethel. He extended the cleanup of false worship beyond Judah.
entries.23:20: He put to death all the priests of those high places on their own altars and burned bones on them, then returned to Jerusalem. He dealt harshly with those who had led people into false worship.
entries.23:21: The king commanded all the people to celebrate the Passover to the Lord as the book of the law said. He wanted them to obey what God had commanded in the rediscovered book.
entries.23:22: No Passover like this one had been kept since the days of the judges or the kings before him. It was an unusually faithful and wholehearted observance.
entries.23:23: This Passover was celebrated to the Lord in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah's reign. It marked a high point of his reforms.
entries.23:24: Josiah removed all the mediums, fortune-tellers, idols, and detestable things from Judah and Jerusalem so that the words of the law would be carried out. He was making the nation's life match what God's book said.
entries.23:25: No king before or after Josiah turned to the Lord with such wholehearted devotion, obeying the law of Moses. He stands out as an example of complete commitment to God.
entries.23:26: Even so, the Lord's fierce anger against Judah was not turned away because of all the evil Manasseh had done. The consequences of earlier sin were still coming.
entries.23:27: The Lord said he would remove Judah from his presence as he had done with Israel, and he would reject Jerusalem and the temple where his name was. The nation's judgment was already determined.
entries.23:28: The rest of Josiah's deeds are recorded in the history book of the kings of Judah. This note points readers to the official records for more details.
entries.23:29: In Josiah's days, the king of Egypt marched against Assyria, and Josiah went out to oppose him and was killed at Megiddo. Even a good king's life ended in a tragic battle.
entries.23:30: His servants carried his body back to Jerusalem and buried him there, and the people made his son Jehoahaz king in his place. The nation mourned and moved on to a new king.
entries.23:31: Jehoahaz was twenty-three when he became king and ruled only three months in Jerusalem; his mother was Hamutal. His reign was very short.
entries.23:32: He did evil in the Lord's eyes, following the example of his ancestors. He did not continue his father's good ways.
entries.23:33: The king of Egypt put him in chains at Riblah so he could not rule in Jerusalem, and he imposed a heavy tax of silver and gold on the land. Foreign power took control and punished the nation.
entries.23:34: Pharaoh made Eliakim king instead of Josiah, changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away to Egypt where he died. The Egyptian king was deciding who ruled Judah.
entries.23:35: Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay the silver and gold Pharaoh demanded, with each person paying what was required. The burden fell on ordinary people to satisfy a foreign ruler.
entries.23:36: Jehoiakim was twenty-five when he became king and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem; his mother was Zebidah. He had a longer reign than his brother.
entries.23:37: He did evil in the Lord's eyes, just as his ancestors had done. Like the kings before him, he turned away from God.
entries.24:1: Judah's king Jehoiakim was forced to serve Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar for three years, then rebelled against him. It shows how quickly a nation's security can collapse when it turns from God.
entries.24:2: God used raiding bands from several neighboring nations to attack Judah and destroy it, exactly as his prophets had warned. God's warnings are not empty; ignoring them brings real consequences.
entries.24:3: Judah's downfall came by God's own decree because of the sins of King Manasseh, removing the people from his presence. Persistent evil eventually brings judgment, even if it takes generations.
entries.24:4: Manasseh had filled Jerusalem with the blood of innocent people, and God would not forgive this. Shedding innocent blood is serious to God and cannot be shrugged off.
entries.24:5: The rest of Jehoiakim's deeds are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings. His story is part of a larger record, reminding us that our actions are remembered.
entries.24:6: Jehoiakim died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Jehoiachin became king. Leadership passes on, but the consequences of a king's choices do not disappear.
entries.24:7: Egypt's king no longer dared to leave his land because Babylon had taken everything from Egypt's border to the Euphrates River. World powers shift, but God remains in control of history.
entries.24:8: Jehoiachin became king at eighteen and ruled only three months; his mother's name is also recorded. A short reign shows how quickly a throne can end when God's judgment comes.
entries.24:9: Jehoiachin did evil in God's eyes, just like his father. Children often repeat their parents' sins, and each person is accountable for following that pattern.
entries.24:10: Nebuchadnezzar's army surrounded Jerusalem and cut it off completely. When God's judgment arrives, there is no escape route.
entries.24:11: Nebuchadnezzar himself came to the city while his troops besieged it. The powerful king personally oversaw Jerusalem's defeat.
entries.24:12: Jehoiachin surrendered to Babylon's king along with his mother, officials, and servants, and was taken captive in Babylon's eighth year. Surrender to an earthly king could not undo the judgment that had already come.
entries.24:13: Nebuchadnezzar looted the temple treasury and cut up the gold vessels Solomon had made, just as God had said. God's warnings about the temple's destruction came true exactly as spoken.
entries.24:14: Babylon carried off Jerusalem's leaders, soldiers, and skilled craftsmen—ten thousand people—leaving only the poorest behind. A nation loses its strength when its capable people are taken away.
entries.24:15: Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon with his mother, wives, servants, and the leading men of the land. Exile separated the king from his home and his people.
entries.24:16: Seven thousand soldiers and a thousand skilled workers were deported to Babylon. The best and strongest of Judah were removed, leaving the land weak and vulnerable.
entries.24:17: Babylon's king made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place and renamed him Zedekiah. The conqueror controlled who ruled, showing that Judah's independence was gone.
entries.24:18: Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and ruled eleven years; his mother's name is recorded too. His long reign gave him many chances to turn back to God.
entries.24:19: Zedekiah did evil in God's eyes, just as Jehoiakim had done. He repeated the same mistakes instead of learning from them.
entries.24:20: God's anger finally led to Jerusalem and Judah being sent away from his presence, and Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon. When people keep refusing God, judgment becomes inevitable, and rebellion only speeds it up.
entries.25:1: Babylon's king brought his whole army to surround Jerusalem and built ramps to attack it. It shows how a powerful enemy closed in on God's city, and reminds us that ignoring God's warnings can lead to hard consequences.
entries.25:2: The siege lasted about a year and a half, cutting the city off from help. For the reader, it shows that a trapped situation can drag on a long time before it finally breaks.
entries.25:3: The food ran out so badly that people had nothing left to eat. It means starvation inside a besieged city, and it shows how desperate life becomes when a crisis goes on too long.
entries.25:4: The soldiers broke through the wall and the king escaped at night through a gate by the garden. It means the defense finally collapsed, and it shows that even a king's escape plan can fail.
entries.25:5: The Babylonian army chased the king and caught him near Jericho, and his soldiers scattered. It means there was no real escape, and it shows that running from a problem often just delays it.
entries.25:6: They captured the king and brought him to the Babylonian king to be judged. It means he had to answer for his rebellion, and it reminds us that leaders are held responsible for their choices.
entries.25:7: They killed his sons in front of him, then blinded him and took him to Babylon in chains. It is a brutal picture of loss and humiliation, and it shows how costly it is to turn away from God.
entries.25:8: About a month later, the Babylonian king's commander came to Jerusalem. It marks the start of the city's destruction, and it shows that judgment came at a set time, not by accident.
entries.25:9: He burned the Lord's temple, the palace, and every important building in Jerusalem. It means the heart of the nation's worship and government was destroyed, and it shows that even sacred places are not safe when people abandon God.
entries.25:10: The Babylonian army tore down the walls around Jerusalem. It means the city was left defenseless, and it shows how complete the collapse was.
entries.25:11: The commander took most of the remaining people and the skilled workers away as prisoners. It means the city was emptied of its people, and it shows the deep loss of being taken from home.
entries.25:12: He left only the poorest people to work the vineyards and fields. It means the land was not completely empty, and it shows that even in judgment God left a small group to keep life going.
entries.25:13: The Babylonians broke up the bronze pillars, stands, and large water basin from the temple and carried the bronze to Babylon. It means the temple's beautiful furnishings were looted, and it shows that wealth and beauty do not protect us from loss.
entries.25:14: They took all the bronze tools and utensils used in the temple service. It means the equipment for worship was carried off, and it shows how thoroughly the nation's religious life was stripped away.
entries.25:15: The commander took the gold and silver bowls and fire pans as well. It means even the precious items were seized, and it shows that nothing valuable was left behind.
entries.25:16: The bronze from the two pillars, the water basin, and the stands was too much to weigh. It means the temple had been richly built, and it shows how much was lost in a single day.
entries.25:17: Each pillar was about twenty-seven feet tall with a decorative bronze top about four and a half feet high. It means these were impressive structures, and it helps the reader picture the scale of what was destroyed.
entries.25:18: The commander arrested the chief priest, the second priest, and the three temple gatekeepers. It means the religious leaders were taken captive, and it shows that no one was exempt from the consequences.
entries.25:19: He also took a court official, five of the king's advisers, the army's record keeper, and sixty other leading men. It means the city's leadership was removed, and it shows that a community loses much when its leaders are taken away.
entries.25:20: The commander brought all these prisoners to the Babylonian king at Riblah. It means they were handed over for judgment, and it shows that the captives had no say in what happened next.
entries.25:21: The Babylonian king had them executed at Riblah in Hamath, and so Judah was taken from its land into exile. It means the nation's leaders were killed and the people were deported, and it marks the sad end of the kingdom of Judah.
entries.25:22: Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah to govern the people who were left in Judah. It means a new local leader was put in charge, and it shows that life went on for those who remained.
entries.25:23: The remaining army officers and their men came to Gedaliah at Mizpah to support him. It means the scattered fighters gathered around the new governor, and it shows a moment of possible stability.
entries.25:24: Gedaliah swore an oath and told them not to fear the Babylonians, but to settle down and serve the king of Babylon, and things would go well. It means he urged peace and cooperation, and it shows that accepting reality can be the wisest path.
entries.25:25: In the seventh month, Ishmael, a member of the royal family, came with ten men and murdered Gedaliah and the Babylonians and Jews with him at Mizpah. It means the peace was shattered by a violent plot, and it shows how one person's ambition can ruin many lives.
entries.25:26: Then everyone, from small to great, fled to Egypt out of fear of the Babylonians. It means the people panicked and left the land, and it shows how fear can drive people away from where God had placed them.
entries.25:27: In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's imprisonment, the new Babylonian king Evil-merodach released him from prison. It means a long captivity finally ended, and it shows that even after decades, God can bring a turn for the better.
entries.25:28: The king spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and gave him a seat higher than the other kings with him in Babylon. It means he was shown honor, and it shows that God had not forgotten the line of David.
entries.25:29: Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate at the king's table every day for the rest of his life. It means he was treated as a guest rather than a prisoner, and it shows a picture of restored dignity.
entries.25:30: The king gave him a regular allowance of food every day for the rest of his life. It means his needs were provided for, and it shows that even in exile, God's care continued.
